title: Resume & One-Pager
what: Build your single-page CV in the standard KGP format. One page is a hard rule, not a target — the format is fixed; your job is to fill it well.
why: Shortlisting at KGP is CV-driven. A weak CV means you never get to show your case skills.
good: One page, no exceptions. Every bullet follows Action → Metric → Impact. No objective statement, no filler, no second page.
mistake: Treating 'one page' as flexible, or listing responsibilities ('worked on X') instead of results ('cut X 30% by doing Y').

tasks.label: Set up your one-page CV in the KGP format
tasks.detail: Follow the standard one-page KGP CV format — section order, one-page limit and bullet density are fixed, not optional. Plenty of good reference templates are a quick search away if you need one. Fill it with your own experience; if it spills to a second page, cut, don't shrink the font.

tasks.label: Run the 10-point bullet audit on every line
tasks.detail: Score every bullet 0/1 on: has a number, has an action verb, states an outcome. Any bullet scoring under 2/3 gets rewritten before you move on.

tasks.label: Get a second pair of eyes on it
tasks.detail: Have someone review it — anyone a step ahead in the same function is ideal, but a peer applying elsewhere works too (they'll catch unclear language even if they don't know the function). If you don't have someone to ask, post it in a placement community or search online for a CV-review checklist and self-audit against it.

trackNotes.consulting:
• Lead with a 3-4 line summary / positioning line (e.g. 'analytical + led teams + quant background') — reviewers scan for a coherent narrative first
• Every bullet: a number AND a structured method (e.g. 'segmented X into Y groups, found Z')
• Call out leadership/ownership scope explicitly — team size, budget, stakeholders managed
• Order: summary → most relevant experience → POR/leadership → skills
trackNotes.product:
• Lead every bullet with a user or business metric, not the feature ('drove 18% activation via X', not 'built X')
• Include at least one line signalling technical fluency (SQL, an experiment, a dashboard) even in a non-technical role
• A teardown, side project or case-comp result earns a line — sometimes ahead of a weaker internship bullet
• Order: summary → product/impact experience → projects → skills
trackNotes.analyst:
• Lead bullets with the named tool/technique, then the outcome ('built a churn model in Python — logistic regression, 0.81 AUC — flagging X% of at-risk users')
• Put a skills line (SQL, Python, Excel, Tableau, key libraries) near the top — it gets scanned first
• Quantify everything; analyst reviewers want specific technical evidence, not just business impact
• Order: skills → analytical experience → projects → education
trackNotes.general:
• Show range, not depth in one function — one operations bullet, one strategy bullet, one people-facing bullet
• Mix business impact, cross-functional exposure and any quantitative bullets you have
• GM roles hire generalists, so a CV that looks narrowly specialised reads worse than one showing breadth
• Order: summary → varied experience → POR → skills

title: Bullet Rewrite Lab
what: A focused rewrite pass turning every weak CV bullet into a quantified, defensible claim.
why: CV deep-dive rounds attack your weakest bullet. Fixing them now removes your softest target.
good: You can defend any bullet for 5 minutes with specifics — the number, the method, the counterfactual.
mistake: Inflating numbers you cannot back up. Interviewers probe exactly the impressive-sounding ones.

tasks.label: Rewrite every bullet using Action-Metric-Impact
tasks.detail: Take every bullet scoring under 2/3 from FOUND-01 and rewrite using Action → Metric → Impact. Aim for one line, 18-22 words.

tasks.label: Write a 5-line defence note under each bullet
tasks.detail: For each bullet write 3-4 lines answering: what was the actual number, how did you measure it, what would have happened without your change.

title: Target Company Map & JD Decode
what: Build your ranked shortlist of target companies and decode what each JD is actually testing.
why: Prep is finite. Knowing that Company A tests SQL and Company B tests guesstimates changes what you study.
good: A ranked sheet: company, role, CTC, test format, interview rounds, your fit gap.
mistake: Preparing generically for 'analytics roles' when three of your targets test three different things.

tasks.label: Build your ranked target sheet from the JD database
tasks.detail: Work through this deliberately rather than skimming — this becomes a reference document you'll return to, so get the structure right the first time.

tasks.label: Map each target to the modules that cover its test format
tasks.detail: Work through this deliberately rather than skimming — this becomes a reference document you'll return to, so get the structure right the first time.

title: Speed Arithmetic
what: Mental math without a calculator: percentages, ratios, fractions, approximations under time pressure.
why: Every OA is time-bound. Slow arithmetic costs you questions you actually knew how to solve.
good: Two-digit multiplication, percentage swings and ratio conversions in under 10 seconds each.
mistake: Practising accuracy without a timer. The OA constraint is speed, not whether you can do it eventually.

tasks.label: Work GFG's aptitude question bank end to end
tasks.detail: This is the comprehensive one — don't cherry-pick topics, go through all of it. Pair it with IndiaBix below for volume.

tasks.label: Drill tables, squares, cubes and reciprocals to 30
tasks.detail: Do the general aptitude section on IndiaBix. Memorise tables to 20, squares to 30, cubes to 20, and reciprocals as percentages — flashcards, not just reading.

tasks.label: Timed sets: every problem under 1 minute
tasks.detail: Analyst-track speed matters most here — build the habit of solving every problem in under a minute, not just eventually getting it right. Cover PrepInsta's aptitude section fully.

tasks.label: Short-trick pass on FacePrep's aptitude articles
tasks.detail: These articles are dense with shortcuts (not just theory) — work through them for the speed tricks, they compound with the tables/squares drilling above.

tasks.label: Log every error into a mistake sheet by type
tasks.detail: Keep a running sheet of every wrong answer tagged by type (percentage / ratio / DI / approximation). After ~30 logged, the pattern in your mistakes becomes obvious and tells you what to drill.

title: Data Interpretation
what: Reading tables, bar charts, pie charts and line graphs fast, then computing what is asked.
why: DI is the single highest-weight section in analyst and consulting OAs.
good: You scan the chart, spot the trap, and answer without recomputing the whole table.
mistake: Calculating exact values when the options are far apart and approximation would have done.

tasks.label: Work through table, bar, pie and line DI sets
tasks.detail: Most people find DI's length intimidating and half-skip it — that's exactly why practising it properly creates a real score gap. Do at least 2 full sets of each chart type.

tasks.label: Timed DI sets: 4 sets in 24 minutes
tasks.detail: 4 sets, 6 minutes each, no calculator. If you're consistently over time, you're calculating exact values where estimation would do.

tasks.label: Build your approximation shortcut sheet
tasks.detail: Write down your go-to shortcuts for 10%, 12.5%, 16.67%, 33.33% conversions and common ratio simplifications — this sheet is what you'll actually use in the exam.

title: Logical Reasoning
what: Arrangements, seating, blood relations, syllogisms, coding-decoding and input-output.
why: LR sections are pure pattern practice — the return per hour is the highest of any OA section.
good: You recognise the set type in 15 seconds and reach for the right grid or diagram immediately.
mistake: Solving in your head. LR sets need a written grid; mental attempts fail on the 4th constraint.

tasks.label: Cover each LR set type with worked examples
tasks.detail: Work through arrangements, seating, blood relations, syllogisms, coding-decoding and input-output — minimum 8 worked examples per type, with a grid drawn for every arrangement question.

tasks.label: Timed mixed LR sets, 3 rounds
tasks.detail: 3 rounds of 15 mixed questions, 20 minutes each. Draw the grid every time, even for easy ones — this builds the habit for when it's hard.

title: Probability & Statistics
what: Counting, conditional probability, Bayes, distributions, expected value and descriptive statistics.
why: Analyst and quant-heavy product OAs lean on this, and it reappears in guesstimate reasoning.
good: You set up the sample space correctly first. Most probability errors are setup errors, not maths errors.
mistake: Jumping to a formula before defining the event. Bayes questions punish this hardest.

tasks.label: Counting, permutations and combinations
tasks.detail: Cover permutations, combinations, and basic counting with at least 15 worked problems — focus on distinguishing when order matters.

tasks.label: Conditional probability and Bayes problem set
tasks.detail: 15 conditional probability problems, minimum 5 on Bayes' theorem specifically. Always draw the sample space or tree before computing — Bayes questions are asked directly in interviews, not just OAs.

tasks.label: Expected value and distribution problems
tasks.detail: Solve 10 expected value problems and cover binomial/normal distribution basics with 5 problems each.

tasks.label: Classic probability puzzle set
tasks.detail: A handful of probability puzzles get reused across interviews and papers (e.g. the classic 'ants on a triangle', answer 1/4). Work through the probability-tagged puzzles on Brainstellar — these aren't in KaseMate's case bank, so practise them on the puzzle sites directly.

title: Advanced DI & Caselets
what: Multi-chart DI, missing-data sets and caselet DI where the data is buried in a paragraph.
why: Top-CTC firms use harder DI as the actual filter. Standard DI practice is not enough for them.
good: You extract a clean table from a paragraph caselet before attempting any question.
mistake: Attempting caselets question-by-question instead of tabulating the whole thing first.

tasks.label: Caselet DI sets — tabulate then solve
tasks.detail: Extract a clean table from the paragraph before attempting any question — don't answer caselets question-by-question.

tasks.label: Missing-data and multi-chart DI sets
tasks.detail: Missing-data and multi-chart DI sets from GFG's harder aptitude sets.

title: Verbal Ability & Reading Comprehension
what: RC strategy, para-jumbles, critical reasoning and error spotting.
why: Consulting and GM OAs carry a verbal section, and RC speed transfers directly to case prompt reading.
good: You read the questions first, skim for structure, and never re-read the passage twice.
mistake: Reading RC passages like a textbook. You need the argument structure, not every detail.

tasks.label: RC sets — 3 passages in 20 minutes
tasks.detail: Read questions first, skim for argument structure, never re-read the whole passage twice. 3 passages, 20 minutes total.

tasks.label: Para-jumbles and critical reasoning drills
tasks.detail: Para-jumbles and critical reasoning drills from GFG's verbal section.

title: Classic Puzzles
what: The standard interview puzzle canon: weighing, crossing, measuring, probability puzzles, chessboard problems.
why: Analyst and quant interviews open with a puzzle. It is a thinking-out-loud test, not a trivia test.
good: You narrate your approach, state assumptions, and recover cleanly when your first idea fails.
mistake: Going silent while you think. The interviewer is grading the process, and silence gives them nothing.

tasks.label: Work through Brainstellar end to end
tasks.detail: This is worth finishing completely, not sampling — it's built around the interview-puzzle format. Puzzles aren't in KaseMate's case bank, so this is your main practice ground for them.

tasks.label: GFG's top 100 interview puzzles
tasks.detail: A second pass at volume once Brainstellar is done.

tasks.label: Record yourself solving 10 puzzles out loud
tasks.detail: Record yourself solving 10 puzzles out loud from the sites above. Narrate every assumption and dead end — the interviewer grades how you think, not just the answer. Track your own progress; there's no in-app puzzle grader.

title: Advanced Puzzles & Brainteasers
what: Harder game-theory, invariant, pigeonhole and strategy puzzles used by quant and top analyst firms.
why: When a firm wants to separate the top 10%, this is the tier of puzzle they reach for.
good: You identify the invariant or the parity argument rather than brute-forcing cases.
mistake: Memorising answers. These get rotated — the pattern of reasoning is what transfers.

tasks.label: Invariants, parity and pigeonhole problem set
tasks.detail: Work the harder Brainstellar tiers plus any invariant/parity problems you can find — these aren't in the case bank, practise on the puzzle sites.

tasks.label: Classic high-difficulty problem collection
tasks.detail: The reasoning patterns (parity, invariants) recur even when exact questions don't, and a few have appeared in OAs. Skip if short on time — not the highest-leverage block.

title: Guesstimates
what: Market sizing and estimation using clean top-down and bottom-up decomposition.
why: Guesstimates appear in almost every non-tech interview across all four tracks.
good: A visible tree, stated assumptions, sane numbers, and a sanity check at the end.
mistake: Producing a number without ever stating the assumptions it rests on.

tasks.label: Learn top-down vs bottom-up with worked examples
tasks.detail: Learn both approaches with a couple of fully worked examples each. Open the Guesstimate set in Browse All — the cases there have structures you can study before drilling.

tasks.label: Practise ~10 guesstimates with written trees
tasks.detail: Work through around 10 from the Guesstimate set, each with a visible tree — population/segment splits, labelled assumptions, and a sanity check against a known number.

tasks.label: Build your India base-numbers sheet
tasks.detail: Build a reference sheet: India's population, urban/rural split, internet/smartphone users, household size, income bands — the numbers every guesstimate needs. This is your own doc.

title: Advanced Market Sizing
what: Sizing with segmentation, penetration curves, replacement cycles and B2B markets.
why: Consulting and strategy rounds push past 'how many autos in Delhi' into real TAM questions.
good: You segment before you estimate and defend each penetration assumption with a reference point.
mistake: Using one blended average across a market that has obviously different segments.

tasks.label: Practise segmented sizing and penetration curves
tasks.detail: Work the harder guesstimates in the Guesstimate set — segment before estimating, defend each penetration assumption with a reference point.

tasks.label: Practise B2B and replacement-cycle sizing
tasks.detail: Continue in the Guesstimate set focusing on B2B and replacement-cycle style sizing.

title: Business Basics
what: Revenue, cost structure, margin, contribution, break-even, CAC, LTV, churn and the core business vocabulary.
why: You cannot structure a profitability case or read a metrics dashboard without this language.
good: You can decompose any business into its revenue and cost drivers within a minute.
mistake: Confusing gross margin with contribution margin, or CAC payback with LTV:CAC.

tasks.label: Learn the core P&L and unit-economics vocabulary
tasks.detail: Learn revenue, COGS, gross margin, contribution margin, fixed vs variable cost, break-even, CAC, LTV, and churn — write your own one-line definition for each, not just the formula.

tasks.label: Decompose 5 real Indian businesses into driver trees
tasks.detail: Pick 5 real Indian businesses (e.g. Zomato, Ola, a D2C brand, a bank, a manufacturer) and draw their revenue and cost driver trees from public information.

title: Indian Business Landscape
what: Who competes with whom across Indian fintech, quick commerce, e-commerce, FMCG and banking.
why: Interviewers pick cases from sectors they hire into. Sector context makes your answers concrete.
good: You can name the players, the business model and the current strategic question in 5 sectors.
mistake: Knowing company names but not their revenue model or their actual competitive pressure.

tasks.label: Build sector one-pagers for 5 target industries
tasks.detail: Apply this to real companies you know, not abstract examples — the concepts stick when tied to something concrete.

tasks.label: Track business news daily for the sectors you target
tasks.detail: Apply this to real companies you know, not abstract examples — the concepts stick when tied to something concrete.

title: Financial Statements & Unit Economics
what: Reading a P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, plus building a unit-economics model.
why: Finance-adjacent roles and profitability cases both assume you can read a statement without help.
good: Given a P&L you can find the margin leak in under two minutes.
mistake: Treating profit and cash flow as the same thing — a classic trap in banking interviews.

tasks.label: Read and dissect 3 real annual-report P&Ls
tasks.detail: Apply this to real companies you know, not abstract examples — the concepts stick when tied to something concrete.

tasks.label: Build a unit-economics model for one company
tasks.detail: Apply this to real companies you know, not abstract examples — the concepts stick when tied to something concrete.

title: SQL Fundamentals
what: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and thinking in sets rather than loops.
why: Every analyst OA and most product-analyst rounds have a live SQL section.
good: You write correct SQL first try, without a syntax hunt, and you can explain what it returns.
mistake: Using WHERE where HAVING is needed. It is the most common single mistake in SQL screens.

tasks.label: Watch the SQL one-shot and take structured notes
tasks.detail: Watch this first, before touching a practice site — it covers SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY in one sitting. Take notes as you go, don't just watch passively.

tasks.label: Revise and go deeper with W3Schools SQL
tasks.detail: Go through the full tutorial for revision and to fill in the depth the video sightly skimmed.

tasks.label: Solve 20 easy query problems, timed
tasks.detail: Very high chance an interviewer hands you a live SQL problem directly from a set like this — solve 20 easy ones from Top SQL 50, under 5 minutes each.

title: Joins & Aggregations
what: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and SELF joins, plus multi-table aggregation and subqueries.
why: Real interview questions are never single-table. Join logic is where candidates actually fail.
good: You reason about row multiplication before writing the join, so counts never surprise you.
mistake: Using an INNER JOIN and silently dropping the rows the question was actually about.

tasks.label: Work through every join type with row-count reasoning
tasks.detail: For every join type, write out on paper what happens to row count before running the query — this is the skill that actually gets tested, not the syntax.

tasks.label: Solve 20 medium multi-table problems
tasks.detail: 20 medium problems from Top SQL 50. For each, identify which join type is needed before writing any SQL.

tasks.label: Extra reps on SQLZoo
tasks.detail: SQLZoo's interactive tutorial is good for join-heavy drilling specifically if LeetCode's problems alone aren't giving you enough join variety.

title: Window Functions
what: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals and PARTITION BY.
why: This is the dividing line between a screening-level and an interview-level SQL candidate.
good: You reach for a window function instead of a self-join when ranking or comparing rows.
mistake: Confusing RANK and DENSE_RANK on tie-handling questions, which is exactly what gets tested.

tasks.label: Learn each window function with worked queries
tasks.detail: Learn ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on tie-handling specifically — write a query that demonstrates the difference on a dataset with ties.

tasks.label: Solve 15 window-function problems
tasks.detail: 15 window function problems covering ranking, running totals, and period-over-period comparison (LAG/LEAD).

title: SQL Case Studies
what: End-to-end business questions answered in SQL: retention cohorts, funnels, DAU/MAU, churn.
why: Senior analyst rounds ask a business question, not a query question. You must translate first.
good: You restate the business question as a table shape before writing a single line of SQL.
mistake: Writing a technically correct query that answers a slightly different question than the one asked.

tasks.label: Build cohort retention and funnel queries end to end
tasks.detail: DataLemur's questions are framed as real business problems, not syntax drills — exactly the translation skill senior analyst rounds test. Build cohort retention and funnel queries.

tasks.label: Solve 10 business-framed SQL case problems
tasks.detail: 10 business-framed SQL case problems from StrataScratch, restating the business question as a table shape before writing any SQL.

title: Python & Pandas
what: Python fundamentals plus pandas: loading, filtering, groupby, merge, pivot and cleaning.
why: Analyst live-coding rounds are almost always pandas, not algorithms.
good: You manipulate a DataFrame fluently without looking up syntax mid-interview.
mistake: Preparing LeetCode DSA when the actual round is a messy CSV and a business question.

tasks.label: Python fundamentals + pandas + intro ML
tasks.detail: Go through the tutorial, the modules section, and the machine learning section — high chance a data-adjacent interview touches all three, even though direct 'write Python from scratch' questions are less common than pandas questions.

tasks.label: Pandas core operations with a real dataset
tasks.detail: Work with a real, messy dataset rather than a clean tutorial one — that's what the actual live-coding round will look like.

title: Pandas for Analyst Cases
what: Applying pandas to open-ended business questions under time pressure.
why: The live round gives you data and 30 minutes. Speed and structure matter more than elegance.
good: You produce a clean answer plus one chart and a spoken insight within the time box.
mistake: Spending 20 minutes on data cleaning and leaving no time for the actual insight.

tasks.label: Timed analysis: dataset to insight in 30 minutes, 4 rounds
tasks.detail: Give yourself a messy dataset and 30 minutes to reach one clean insight plus a chart — four rounds. The live analyst round is exactly this: speed and a clear finding matter more than elegant code.

tasks.label: Build a reusable cleaning and EDA snippet file
tasks.detail: Save your go-to pandas snippets — loading, null-handling, groupby, quick plots — into one file you can paste from. In a timed round, not re-typing boilerplate buys you minutes for the actual analysis.

title: A/B Testing & Experimentation
what: Hypothesis testing, p-values, power, sample size, and how experiments actually get designed.
why: Product-analyst and DS rounds test experiment design more reliably than they test modelling.
good: You state the metric, the hypothesis, the unit of randomisation and the guardrails, in that order.
mistake: Talking about significance without ever defining the success metric or the randomisation unit.

tasks.label: Hypothesis testing, power and sample size
tasks.detail: Learn hypothesis testing, p-values, power and sample size on Kaggle Learn. State the metric, hypothesis, randomisation unit and guardrails in that order.

tasks.label: Design 5 experiments end to end
tasks.detail: Design 5 experiments for real products on paper — metric, hypothesis, unit of randomisation, guardrails. A/B design isn't in the case bank, so this is a written self-exercise you can review with a peer.

title: Regression & ML Basics
what: Linear and logistic regression, overfitting, train-test split, and the standard evaluation metrics.
why: DS-adjacent analyst roles ask you to interpret a model, not to build one from scratch.
good: You can read a coefficient, explain what it means in business terms, and name its limitation.
mistake: Reciting algorithm names without being able to interpret a single coefficient or metric.

tasks.label: Machine learning fundamentals, one focused pass
tasks.detail: This single ~6 hour video covers most of the core ML algorithms in one sitting — good for building a first working mental model before going deeper.

tasks.label: Go deeper with a structured ML playlist
tasks.detail: Covers more ground than the single video above, including some applied projects — use this for depth once the fundamentals from the first video are solid.

tasks.label: Classification metrics: precision, recall, ROC-AUC
tasks.detail: Given a P&L you can find the margin leak in under two minutes — same idea here: given a confusion matrix you should be able to state precision, recall and the trade-off in under a minute.

title: Excel & Spreadsheet Modelling
what: Lookups, pivots, conditional aggregation and building a clean model layout.
why: Consulting and GM roles still run Excel tests, and many analyst rounds allow only a spreadsheet.
good: Your model has separate input, calculation and output blocks and no hardcoded numbers in formulas.
mistake: Burying assumptions inside formulas so nothing can be sensitivity-tested.

tasks.label: Lookups, pivots and conditional aggregation drills
tasks.detail: Build something functional, not just following a tutorial — a real dashboard or model teaches the decisions a tutorial skips.

tasks.label: Build one clean 3-block financial model
tasks.detail: Build something functional, not just following a tutorial — a real dashboard or model teaches the decisions a tutorial skips.

title: Dashboards & Data Storytelling
what: Choosing the right chart, building a dashboard, and structuring an insight narrative.
why: Analyst take-homes are graded on communication as much as on correctness.
good: One headline insight per chart, and the dashboard answers a question rather than displaying data.
mistake: Building a dashboard with 12 charts and no stated conclusion.

tasks.label: Chart selection and dashboard structure
tasks.detail: Build something functional, not just following a tutorial — a real dashboard or model teaches the decisions a tutorial skips.

tasks.label: Build one dashboard on a real dataset with a written narrative
tasks.detail: Build something functional, not just following a tutorial — a real dashboard or model teaches the decisions a tutorial skips.

title: Engineering & Quant Maths
what: Fourier series, Laplace transforms, complex numbers, integration and other engineering-maths topics that show up in quant-leaning OAs.
why: Global banks and quant-heavy recruiters (GS, JPMorgan, HSBC-style roles) sometimes test JEE-level engineering maths, not just business aptitude — this is a narrow but real gap if you skip it.
good: You can solve a standard Laplace transform or complex-number problem at the speed you'd expect from second-year engineering coursework, without relearning it from scratch under time pressure.
mistake: Preparing this like a fresh subject. It's revision, not new learning — treat it as knocking the rust off JEE-level material you've already seen.

tasks.label: MCQ practice across engineering maths topics
tasks.detail: Covers Fourier series, Laplace transforms, complex numbers, integration and more in MCQ form — only worth doing if a target company on your list is known for this style of test (typically the larger global quant/banking recruiters, not most Indian fintech or product firms).

title: Case Interview Mechanics
what: The universal shape of a case: clarify, structure, analyse, synthesise, recommend.
why: Every track gets cased. Mechanics are what let you look composed before you know the answer.
good: You always clarify first, structure on paper, and close with a recommendation plus risks.
mistake: Diving into analysis before restating the objective, then solving the wrong problem well.

tasks.label: Learn the 5-step case flow from a walkthrough
tasks.detail: The case flow (clarify, structure, analyse, synthesise, recommend) is best learned from an annotated walkthrough — the Exponent playlist covers it well. A quick search for 'consulting case interview framework' turns up plenty more. Learn the shape here first.

tasks.label: Practise clarifying + structuring on ~10 cases
tasks.detail: Open the Profitability set in Browse All and work the opening — clarifying questions and structure — on about 10 cases. Don't worry about the final number yet, just the setup.

tasks.label: Run a few full cases focusing only on structure
tasks.detail: Run a few full cases with a clean structure as your only goal. Use the live Practice mode for one or two of these, and read through the rest in Browse All.

title: Profitability Cases
what: Diagnosing why profit fell using a revenue and cost decomposition tree.
why: Profitability is the most frequently asked consulting case type by a wide margin.
good: You isolate whether it is a revenue or cost problem before going one level deeper.
mistake: Listing every possible cause instead of narrowing with data at each branch.

tasks.label: Learn the profitability tree
tasks.detail: Learn the revenue-cost profitability tree and its volume-price-mix variant from a worked example — the Exponent walkthrough covers it, and searching 'profitability case framework' brings up more. Then practise in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise ~10 profitability cases
tasks.detail: The single most common consulting case type — worth the most reps. Open the Profitability set in Browse All and work through around 10, using live Practice mode for a couple and reading the rest.

tasks.label: See where you're slipping and fix it
tasks.detail: Check the Performance page to see which part of your cases keeps costing you marks, and target that next.

title: Market Entry Cases
what: Should the client enter this market — sizing, attractiveness, capability fit and entry mode.
why: The second-most common consulting case type and a favourite in GM interviews too.
good: You size the market, test attractiveness and capability, then pick an entry mode with a reason.
mistake: Sizing the market beautifully and then never answering whether to actually enter.

tasks.label: Learn the market entry framework
tasks.detail: Learn the market-entry framework and entry modes from a worked case — the Exponent playlist or a quick search for 'market entry case framework' both work. Then practise in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise ~10 market entry cases
tasks.detail: The other highest-frequency case type. Open the Market Entry set in Browse All and work through around 10.

tasks.label: See where you're slipping and fix it
tasks.detail: Check the Performance page for your recurring gap and target it.

title: M&A and Pricing Cases
what: Acquisition rationale, valuation logic, synergies, and the three pricing approaches.
why: Mid and late consulting rounds move here once you have cleared profitability and entry.
good: On pricing you name cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based, then justify your choice.
mistake: Treating an M&A case as a market entry case and skipping synergy and integration risk.

tasks.label: Learn M&A rationale and pricing approaches
tasks.detail: Learn deal rationale, synergies, integration risk, and the three pricing approaches (cost-plus, competitor, value-based). The Exponent playlist and a search for 'pricing case framework' cover these.

tasks.label: Practise a few M&A / growth cases
tasks.detail: Open the M&A / Growth Strategy set in Browse All. A few solid reps is plenty — lighter-coverage type than profitability and market entry, so don't over-invest.

tasks.label: Practise a few pricing cases
tasks.detail: Open the Pricing set in Browse All and do a couple, naming the pricing approach before solving.

title: Growth & Market Share Cases
what: How to grow revenue or win share — organic levers, channel, segment and competitive response.
why: Growth cases show up constantly in GM and strategy interviews at Indian corporates.
good: You separate market growth from share growth before proposing anything.
mistake: Proposing a list of growth ideas with no prioritisation and no view of competitor reaction.

tasks.label: Learn growth-lever and share frameworks
tasks.detail: Separate market growth from share growth before proposing anything. Learn the frameworks from the Exponent playlist or a quick search for 'growth strategy case'.

tasks.label: Practise a few growth cases
tasks.detail: Open the M&A / Growth Strategy set in Browse All — it covers growth-strategy cases. A few solid reps here.

title: Operations & Supply Chain Cases
what: Capacity, bottlenecks, inventory, throughput and cost-to-serve.
why: Manufacturing and FMCG recruiters at KGP lean heavily on operations cases.
good: You find the bottleneck first, because everything upstream of it is not the problem.
mistake: Optimising a non-bottleneck step, which improves nothing in total throughput.

tasks.label: Learn bottleneck and throughput frameworks
tasks.detail: Find the bottleneck first — everything upstream isn't the problem. Learn the frameworks from the Exponent playlist or a search for 'operations case framework'. As an IE student, lean into this one.

tasks.label: Practise a few operations cases
tasks.detail: Open the Operations set in Browse All and work through a few.

title: Unconventional & Public Sector Cases
what: Non-profit, government, social impact and cases with no obvious framework.
why: Firms use these specifically to see whether you can structure without a memorised template.
good: You build a bespoke structure from the objective rather than forcing a known framework.
mistake: Jamming a profitability tree onto a case where the objective is not profit at all.

tasks.label: Learn to structure without frameworks
tasks.detail: Non-profit, government and no-framework cases test whether you can build a bespoke structure from the objective. Search 'non-standard case interview' for worked examples — there's no dedicated set for these in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise bespoke structuring on operations cases
tasks.detail: The Operations set in Browse All has the most open-ended prompts — use it to practise structuring from the objective rather than a template.

title: Product Design
what: Design a product for a user — user segmentation, pain points, solutions, prioritisation, metrics.
why: The single most common PM interview question format across every product company.
good: You pick one segment and go deep rather than covering three segments shallowly.
mistake: Jumping to features before establishing who the user is and what pain you are solving.

tasks.label: Learn the CIRCLES-style design flow
tasks.detail: The Exponent PM playlist walks through the design-question flow. Learn it before drilling.

tasks.label: Watch the mock-interview breakdowns in the key-concepts playlist
tasks.detail: This 25-video playlist covers various PM interview topics — look specifically for the mock-interview and design-question breakdown videos, which walk through a live answer being built and critiqued in real time.

tasks.label: Practise ~8 product design questions
tasks.detail: The most common PM format. Open the Product Design set in Browse All and work through around 8 — pick one user segment per case and go deep.

tasks.label: See where you're slipping and fix it
tasks.detail: Check the Performance page and target your weakest step next.

tasks.label: Read a product-interview prep book
tasks.detail: "Decode and Conquer" (Lewis C. Lin) and "The Product Manager Interview" (also Lewis C. Lin) are the two most widely recommended PM-interview books, followed by "Cracking the PM Interview". Treat this as background reading spread across the plan, not a one-sitting task — buy, borrow, or find a copy online.

title: RCA & Metrics
what: Metric dropped — diagnose it. Segment, isolate, test hypotheses, and define the right metrics.
why: RCA is the highest-signal PM and product-analyst question and it is asked constantly.
good: You rule out instrumentation and seasonality before hunting for a product cause.
mistake: Guessing causes at random instead of segmenting systematically by dimension.

tasks.label: Learn the RCA decomposition and metric frameworks
tasks.detail: Rule out instrumentation and seasonality before hunting a product cause. Learn the RCA framework from the key-concepts playlist, then practise in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise ~8 RCA and metrics questions
tasks.detail: Highest-signal PM/analyst question type. Open the Metrics / Root-Cause set in Browse All and work through around 8.

tasks.label: See where you're slipping and fix it
tasks.detail: Check the Performance page and target recurring gaps.

title: Prioritisation & Roadmapping
what: Choosing what to build — RICE, impact-effort, and defending trade-offs under constraints.
why: Every PM round contains a trade-off question, often disguised inside a design question.
good: You state your prioritisation criteria before ranking, so the ranking is defensible.
mistake: Naming a framework and then ranking by gut feel anyway.

tasks.label: Learn RICE and impact-effort prioritisation
tasks.detail: State your prioritisation criteria before ranking. Learn RICE and impact-effort from the key-concepts playlist.

tasks.label: Practise the prioritisation cases
tasks.detail: Open the Prioritization / Tradeoff set in Browse All and work through it, then supplement below.

tasks.label: Add a prioritisation angle to a few design cases
tasks.detail: Revisit a few Product Design cases you've done and force a ranked prioritisation decision with a stated criterion.

title: Product Teardowns
what: Analysing a live product: what it does well, what it misses, and what you would change.
why: Teardowns are asked directly and they also give you concrete examples for every other answer.
good: You anchor critique in a user segment and a metric, not in personal taste.
mistake: Listing UI nitpicks with no hypothesis about why the team made that choice.

tasks.label: Learn the teardown structure
tasks.detail: Learn the teardown structure from the key-concepts playlist — anchor critique in a user segment and metric, not taste.

tasks.label: Study a few real PM decks
tasks.detail: Search LinkedIn for Flipkart / HiLabs / Tata 1mg-style PM decks people have shared publicly. Analyse the flow — everything on a slide is there for a reason. Searching '<company> PM case deck' surfaces plenty.

tasks.label: Recreate one deck, then build your own from scratch
tasks.detail: Copy one deck slide-for-slide in Figma to learn the tool and design language, then build a completely original deck for the same problem and compare.

tasks.label: Practise teardown-style cases
tasks.detail: Open the Product Improvement set in Browse All — it's the closest to teardown practice. Drill written teardowns of Indian apps here.

tasks.label: Present one teardown out loud in 8 minutes
tasks.detail: Record and present one teardown in 8 minutes. Watch it back and self-review.

title: Product Strategy Cases
what: Should we enter this space, build vs buy, competitive response and platform strategy.
why: Senior PM and APM final rounds move from design into strategy questions.
good: You connect the strategic choice back to the company's actual moat and monetisation.
mistake: Answering strategy questions with feature ideas instead of positioning and economics.

tasks.label: Learn product strategy frameworks
tasks.detail: Connect strategic choices to the company's moat and monetisation, not features. Learn from the key-concepts playlist.

tasks.label: Practise a few product strategy questions
tasks.detail: Open the Strategy / Go-to-Market set in Browse All and work through a few.

title: Execution & Trade-offs
what: Launch planning, go/no-go decisions, estimation, and handling ambiguity with incomplete data.
why: Execution rounds test whether you can actually ship, not just whether you can ideate.
good: You name the decision, the data you would need, and what you would do without it.
mistake: Asking for more data and stopping there instead of committing to a decision under uncertainty.

tasks.label: Learn launch, go/no-go and estimation frameworks
tasks.detail: Execution rounds test whether you can ship, not just ideate. Learn the frameworks from the key-concepts playlist.

tasks.label: Practise execution-style cases
tasks.detail: Open the Product Improvement set in Browse All — it has the closest go/no-go style prompts. Practise committing to a decision under incomplete data.

title: Technical Fluency for PMs
what: APIs, databases, latency, caching, system design at a PM level of depth.
why: Tech-company PM rounds check that you can hold a credible conversation with engineers.
good: You explain a system at the right altitude and know what you do not know.
mistake: Bluffing depth. Engineers spot it instantly and it costs you more than admitting the gap.

tasks.label: Learn the core technical concepts a PM must hold
tasks.detail: APIs, databases, latency, caching, system design at PM depth. No case set for this — learn the concepts (a search for 'system design for PMs' is a good start) and be able to say what you don't know.

tasks.label: Explain 5 product architectures out loud
tasks.detail: Pick 5 products you use and explain their architecture out loud at the right altitude. Self-assess.

title: Metrics Design & North Star
what: Choosing a north star, building metric trees, and designing guardrails.
why: Both PM and analyst interviews ask 'what would you measure' in almost every round.
good: Your north star reflects delivered user value, not just activity, and has guardrails.
mistake: Picking a vanity metric like total signups that can go up while the product gets worse.

tasks.label: Learn north-star and metric-tree construction
tasks.detail: For every metric, know what gaming it looks like. Learn metric-tree construction from the key-concepts playlist.

tasks.label: Practise metric design on RCA cases
tasks.detail: Open the Metrics / Root-Cause set in Browse All to practise defining north-star metrics and guardrails for real products.

title: GD & WAT Playbook
what: Group discussion tactics and written ability test structure under time pressure.
why: Consulting and GM shortlists at KGP frequently include a GD or WAT elimination round.
good: You enter early with a structure, bring in quiet members, and summarise at the end.
mistake: Fighting for airtime volume. Assessors grade contribution quality and group behaviour.

tasks.label: Learn GD roles, entry lines and summarising
tasks.detail: Learn how to enter a GD early with structure, bring in quiet members, and summarise at the end. Searching 'group discussion tips MBA' brings up plenty; the key-concepts playlist also helps. This isn't something KaseMate simulates — practise it live.

tasks.label: Write 5 timed WAT essays, 20 minutes each
tasks.detail: Write five WAT essays under a 20-minute timer each. Do these on paper or a doc and self-review against a structure — KaseMate doesn't grade WAT.

title: Sales, Marketing & Brand Cases
what: Distribution, channel strategy, brand positioning, 4Ps and go-to-market for FMCG-type firms.
why: ITC, HUL-style and bank GM roles case you on distribution and brand, not on profitability trees.
good: You reason about channel economics and trade margins, not just consumer messaging.
mistake: Answering a distribution question with an advertising campaign idea.

tasks.label: Learn channel, distribution and 4P frameworks
tasks.detail: GM roles case you on distribution and brand, not profitability trees. Learn channel economics, trade margins and the 4Ps — searching 'FMCG distribution case' or 'marketing case framework' brings up plenty. There's no dedicated GM set in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise using Market Entry as the closest proxy
tasks.detail: KaseMate's bank is consulting/product cases, so use the Market Entry set in Browse All as the closest structured proxy for GM-style reps, and supplement with FMCG/brand cases you find online.

title: Manufacturing & Plant Cases
what: Plant-level problem solving: efficiency, quality, safety, workforce and cost reduction.
why: Tata Steel and similar core recruiters case you on shop-floor problems, and you are IE — lean into it.
good: You connect your IE coursework and internship directly to the plant problem in front of you.
mistake: Answering like a strategy consultant when the interviewer wants operational specifics.

tasks.label: Learn plant efficiency and quality frameworks
tasks.detail: Tata Steel-style recruiters case you on shop-floor problems. As an IE student, connect your coursework directly. Search 'manufacturing / operations case' for worked examples — no dedicated set in KaseMate.

tasks.label: Practise using Operations as the closest proxy
tasks.detail: Use the Operations set in Browse All as the closest proxy for manufacturing-case reps, and supplement with plant cases you find online.

title: Resume Deep-Dive Interview
what: Defending every line of your CV under sustained follow-up questioning.
why: The CV round is the most predictable round you will face, which makes failing it unforgivable.
good: You have a 2-minute and a 30-second version of every project, with numbers ready.
mistake: Being fluent on your best project and vague on the one they happen to pick.

tasks.label: Write STAR narratives for every CV line
tasks.detail: Write a 2-minute and 30-second version of every project with numbers ready. There's no CV-round simulator in KaseMate — rehearse out loud, record yourself, or run it with a peer.

tasks.label: Run a full CV grilling
tasks.detail: Get someone to attack your weakest bullet with follow-ups, or record yourself answering likely probes. Searching 'CV deep dive interview questions' gives you a bank to drill against.

title: HR & Behavioural Bank
what: The standard behavioural set — tell me about yourself, strengths, weaknesses, why this role.
why: Behavioural answers are graded on structure and specificity, and they are fully preparable.
good: Every answer is a specific story with a result, delivered in under 90 seconds.
mistake: Generic answers with no story. 'I am a hard worker' is worth nothing without evidence.

tasks.label: Build your story bank — 10 stories, STAR format
tasks.detail: Write 10 stories covering leadership, failure, conflict, teamwork and initiative from your SaveSage, Product Club and Inter IIT experience. Your own doc.

tasks.label: Rehearse 20 standard HR questions out loud
tasks.detail: Rehearse the standard behavioural questions under 90 seconds each. The key-concepts playlist has framing tips, and searching 'common HR interview questions' gives the full list to drill.

title: Advanced Behavioural
what: Conflict, failure, leadership, ethical dilemmas and the multi-layer follow-up chains that follow.
why: The first answer is easy. The third follow-up is where candidates fall apart.
good: You own failures without deflecting, and you name what you changed afterwards.
mistake: Choosing a fake weakness or a failure that was secretly someone else's fault.

tasks.label: Prepare conflict, failure and leadership stories
tasks.detail: Own your failures without deflecting; name what you changed. Prepare these as written notes.

tasks.label: Run follow-up chain drills — 3 layers deep
tasks.detail: Have someone push each answer three follow-ups deep, or write out the likely follow-up chain yourself and prepare for it. This is where candidates fall apart.

title: Company Research & Why Us
what: Researching a company well enough to give a specific, non-interchangeable 'why us' answer.
why: A generic 'why us' is the fastest way to signal that you would take any offer.
good: You reference something specific — a recent move, a product decision, a team — and tie it to you.
mistake: Reciting the company's About page back at the person who works there.

tasks.label: Build research one-pagers for your top 5 targets
tasks.detail: Build a one-pager per target company: what they do, recent strategic moves (last 6 months), the team/role you're applying to, and one open question you'd genuinely ask them.

tasks.label: Draft and rehearse a distinct 'why us' for each
tasks.detail: Write a 60-90 second 'why us' answer per company that references something specific from your one-pager — not the About page.

title: Shortlist Dossiers
what: Deep dossiers on the companies you actually get shortlisted for — process, panel, past questions.
why: Once shortlists are out, targeted prep beats generic prep by a wide margin.
good: You know each shortlisted company's round structure, its typical case types, and the questions it tends to ask — all of which is findable online.
mistake: Preparing identically for all shortlists when their formats differ completely.

tasks.label: Build a full dossier per shortlisted company
tasks.detail: Build a dossier per shortlisted company — round structure, panel, past questions. Search '<company> interview experience' and placement forums; this info is public and easy to find.

tasks.label: Practise cases in your company's favoured type
tasks.detail: Filter Browse All to the case type your shortlisted company favours (Profitability for most consulting; switch to Product Design or Metrics/Root-Cause for product roles) and work through a handful.

title: Full-Length Case Practice
what: Doing complete cases end to end in KaseMate's AI interview mode, under realistic conditions.
why: Solo reading hides your real failure modes. Only a full timed case in interview mode surfaces them.
good: You complete the case in time, stay composed under the AI's follow-ups, and act on the feedback.
mistake: Delaying your first full case until you 'feel ready'. You never will — start now.

tasks.label: Do 2 full cases in AI interview mode
tasks.detail: Run a couple of complete cases end to end in KaseMate's Practice mode — the AI runs it like an interview with follow-ups. No pausing.

tasks.label: Record yourself doing one case and review it
tasks.detail: After a full case, check the Performance page to see how you scored across dimensions and where you lost marks.

tasks.label: Log your top 3 failure modes
tasks.detail: Write down the 3 mistakes that keep recurring across your cases — this becomes your focus for the next couple of weeks.

title: Review & Self-Correction
what: Doing cases, then reviewing your own performance to fix delivery as well as content.
why: Pace, filler words and structure are invisible to you until you review the session.
good: You cut filler and hit a clear signposted structure the listener can follow.
mistake: Doing cases and never reviewing them — the review is the entire point.

tasks.label: Do 3 full cases in Practice mode
tasks.detail: Run three complete cases in KaseMate's interview mode, back to back where you can.

tasks.label: Review your scores and delivery on Performance
tasks.detail: Go through the Performance page for each case — score yourself on structure, delivery and pace, and note what to fix.

title: Back-to-Back Case Stamina
what: Doing several cases in a row to build the stamina a real interview day demands.
why: Real interview days are stamina tests — performing well on case 1 and fading by case 3 is common.
good: Your third case is as structured as your first.
mistake: Only ever doing single cases, then fading during the real multi-round day.

tasks.label: Do 3 cases back-to-back in one sitting
tasks.detail: Run three cases in a row in Practice mode with no long breaks — this builds the endurance the real day needs.

tasks.label: Repeat with a different case type
tasks.detail: Do it again with a different case category so you're not only sharp on one type.

title: Case Sprint I — Volume Block
what: A structured volume block: 10 full cases across your track's main types, logged and reviewed.
why: Frameworks become fluent through repetition. There is no substitute for case volume.
good: You complete 10 cases and can name the pattern in your mistakes across all of them.
mistake: Doing cases without reviewing them, so you repeat the same structural error ten times.

tasks.label: Work a volume block of full cases
tasks.detail: Do a solid block of complete cases across your track's main types in KaseMate's Practice mode. Switch categories as you go.

tasks.label: Review scores and spot your pattern
tasks.detail: Check the Performance page after the block — the goal is to name the one mistake that recurs across all of them.

title: Weakness Drill Sprint
what: A targeted block attacking only your lowest-scoring dimension from the Performance page.
why: Late-stage gains come from fixing your weakest dimension, not repeating your strongest.
good: Your weakest radar dimension moves up measurably by the end of the block.
mistake: Practising what you enjoy. Your comfortable case type is not the one costing you offers.

tasks.label: Find your weakest dimension
tasks.detail: Open the Performance page radar to see your lowest-scoring dimension.

tasks.label: Do a focused block on that weakness
tasks.detail: Filter to cases that stress your weakest dimension and work a focused block on just those in Practice mode.

tasks.label: Confirm the movement on Performance
tasks.detail: Re-check the radar after the block and confirm your weakest dimension has moved up.

title: Peer Mock Marathon
what: Partner mocks where you alternate interviewing and being interviewed.
why: Giving cases teaches you what interviewers actually notice. It is the fastest late-stage upgrade.
good: You run a clean case as the interviewer and give specific, structured feedback.
mistake: Only ever being the candidate. Interviewing is where the grading logic becomes visible.

tasks.label: Run peer mocks, alternating roles
tasks.detail: Pair with a batchmate and alternate interviewing each other — being the interviewer is the fastest way to see the grading logic. Case-prep communities online will pair you if you don't have a partner.

tasks.label: Consolidate all feedback into a fix list
tasks.detail: Log every session in Performance afterward. Volume without review just repeats the same mistake at higher speed.

title: Final Sweep & Interview Readiness
what: The last pass: revise your story bank, run light cases to stay warm, and prepare logistics.
why: The week before interviews is for sharpening and confidence, not for new material.
good: You are warm, rested, and your notes fit on two pages you can skim before each round.
mistake: Cramming new frameworks in the final week, which adds anxiety and displaces what you know.

tasks.label: Condense everything into a 2-page skim sheet
tasks.detail: Pull your frameworks and story bank into a 2-page sheet you can skim before each round. Your own doc.

tasks.label: Do a few light warm-up cases
tasks.detail: Run a few easy cases in Practice mode to stay sharp — this week is for staying warm, not new material.

tasks.label: Prepare your questions for the interviewer
tasks.detail: Write the questions you'll ask each interviewer. Your own doc.
